sourceTitle: Space Radiation — NASA Human Spaceflight Hazards
researchSummary: Space radiation is significantly more energetic and hazardous than terrestrial radiation, consisting of Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR), Solar Particle Events (SPE), and trapped radiation belts. Outside Earth's protective magnetosphere, astronauts face increased lifetime risks of cancer, central nervous system impairment, degenerative tissue effects, and acute radiation syndromes.
limitations: Individual biological susceptibility varies widely based on genetic background, age, and mission duration. Deep-space biological responses to heavy ion GCR flux remain an area of ongoing active research.
attribution: NASA Human Research Program (2024). Hazards of Human Spaceflight: Space Radiation. National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

sourceTitle: Isolation and Confinement — NASA Human Spaceflight Hazards
researchSummary: Prolonged confinement in confined space habitats with small crew complements during exploration missions induces circadian desynchronization, chronic stress, mood disturbances, sleep deprivation, and interpersonal friction. Behavioral health degradation directly threatens crew cohesion and executive task performance.
limitations: Observational analog studies (e.g., HERA, NEK, Antarctic stations) provide high psychological fidelity but cannot fully recreate the true existential isolation of interplanetary space.
attribution: NASA Human Research Program (2024). Hazards of Human Spaceflight: Isolation and Confinement. National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

sourceTitle: Distance from Earth — NASA Human Spaceflight Hazards
researchSummary: Transit to Mars involves one-way communication latency of up to 22 minutes and precludes emergency medical evacuation to Earth. Medical care, physiological monitoring, and operational interventions must transition entirely from ground-dependent mission control telemedicine to autonomous onboard crew intelligence systems.
limitations: Autonomous clinical algorithms must balance conservative monitoring with low false-positive rates to avoid alarm fatigue in isolated environments.
attribution: NASA Human Research Program (2024). Hazards of Human Spaceflight: Distance from Earth. National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

sourceTitle: Gravity Fields — NASA Human Spaceflight Hazards
researchSummary: Astronauts encounter variable gravitational regimes (weightlessness, Lunar 0.16g, Martian 0.38g, and hypergravity during transit maneuvers). Microgravity induces cephalad fluid shifts, cardiovascular deconditioning, orthostatic intolerance upon re-gravitation, loss of bone mineral density (~1-1.5% per month), and Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).
limitations: Ground head-down tilt (HDT) bed rest studies simulate axial fluid shifts and disuse but do not replicate gravitational gradient transitions or Coriolis accelerations.
attribution: NASA Human Research Program (2024). Hazards of Human Spaceflight: Gravity Fields. National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

sourceTitle: Hostile/Closed Environments — NASA Human Spaceflight Hazards
researchSummary: Space habitats are sealed, closed-loop environmental control and life support ecosystems (ECLSS). Elevated ambient CO2 concentrations (often 10x terrestrial ambient levels), acoustic noise, recycled air and water, microbial shifts, and potential toxic leaks pose continuous physiological burdens.
limitations: Environmental thresholds established for 1g industrial settings do not account for synergistic microgravity fluid shifts and physiological sensitivity changes.
attribution: NASA Human Research Program (2024). Hazards of Human Spaceflight: Hostile/Closed Environments. National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

sourceTitle: Risk of Cardiac Rhythm Problems and Orthostatic Intolerance
researchSummary: Microgravity eliminates hydrostatic blood pressure gradients, causing an immediate upward fluid shift of approximately 1.5 to 2 liters of blood and interstitial fluid. This triggers reflex diuresis, plasma volume reduction, baroreceptor resetting, and cardiac remodeling, elevating risks of arrhythmias and post-landing orthostatic intolerance.
limitations: Observational telemetry during long-duration ISS increments shows wide inter-individual variability in autonomic vascular tone recovery.
attribution: NASA HRP Cardiovascular Discipline (2023). Human Research Program Risk Report: Cardiac Rhythm Problems. NASA Johnson Space Center.

sourceTitle: Risk of Performance Decrements Associated with Sleep Loss and Work Overload
researchSummary: Astronauts in orbital flight routinely achieve only 6.0 to 6.4 hours of sleep per night compared to >7.5 hours baseline on Earth. Microgravity sleeping arrangements, circadian disruptions (16 sunrises/sunsets every 24 hours in LEO), cabin acoustic noise, and intense operational tempos result in acute and chronic sleep debt and elevated fatigue ratings.
limitations: Subjective fatigue scores may underestimate acute cognitive decrements due to astronaut mission motivation and adrenaline during high-criticality tasks.
attribution: NASA HRP Behavioral Health & Performance (2023). Human Research Program Risk Report: Sleep Loss and Circadian Desynchronization. NASA JSC.

sourceTitle: Risk of Acute and Chronic Carbon Dioxide (CO2) Toxicity in Spaceflight
researchSummary: In weightlessness, absence of natural thermal convection allows pockets of exhaled CO2 to accumulate around sleeping or sedentary crewmembers ('CO2 bubbles'). Elevated cabin CO2 has been epidemiologically linked to astronaut headaches, lethargy, cognitive decrements, and may exacerbate cephalad venous congestion linked to SANS.
limitations: Individual susceptibility to mild hypercapnia varies; localized pocket measurements differ from bulk module ECLSS sensor telemetry.
attribution: NASA HRP Habitability & Environmental Factors (2023). Evidence Report: Risk of Adverse Health Effects from In-Flight Carbon Dioxide Exposure. NASA JSC.

sourceTitle: NASA Spaceflight Standard Measures: Cardiovascular Assessment Protocol
researchSummary: Defines standardized, longitudinal cardiovascular measurement protocols for all ISS expedition crewmembers. Prescribes resting heart rate, blood pressure, Holter ECG ambulatory monitoring for heart rate variability (SDNN, RMSSD), and 24-hour arterial stiffness evaluation collected pre-flight (L-180, L-60), in-flight (FD15, FD60, FD120, R-15), and post-flight (R+3, R+30).
limitations: Protocol adheres to non-invasive operational constraints aboard ISS; full arterial cannulation is clinically prohibitive in operational flight.
attribution: NASA Human Research Program Standard Measures Project (2024). Standard Measures Cardiovascular Protocol Definition. NASA Johnson Space Center.

sourceTitle: NASA Spaceflight Standard Measures: Sleep & Behavioral Health Protocol
researchSummary: Specifies mandatory continuous actigraphy monitoring (Actiwatch / wearable accelerometry), daily subjective sleep logs (sleep latency, wake episodes, sleep quality), Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS), and periodic Visual Analog Scales (VAS) for stress and mood state evaluation.
limitations: Wrist actigraphy algorithms calibrated for terrestrial 1g movement occasionally require manual sleep log reconciliation due to microgravity sleeping posture.
attribution: NASA Human Research Program Standard Measures Project (2024). Standard Measures Sleep, Actigraphy and Behavioral Protocol. NASA JSC.

sourceTitle: OSDR RadLab Database and Space Radiation Telemetry API
researchSummary: The OSDR RadLab portal and API aggregate calibrated space radiation physics telemetry from international space agency detectors onboard the ISS, Artemis trajectory hardware, and ground facilities. Captures absorbed dose rates (µGy/h), dose equivalent rates (µSv/h), flux, and orbital coordinates across modules.
limitations: Telemetry originates from active physical detectors (DOSTEL, REM, Liulin) rather than in-vivo biological biodosimeters; tissue-equivalent dose requires RBE quality weighting.
attribution: NASA Open Science Data Repository (2024). RadLab Space Radiation Portal and API. NASA Ames Research Center.

sourceTitle: OSDR Environmental Data App: ISS Life Support Telemetry
researchSummary: Provides open access to verified International Space Station cabin and payload enclosure environmental parameters including cabin temperature (°C), carbon dioxide levels (%), ambient pressure (kPa), and relative humidity (%) across mission increments.
limitations: Environmental sensors reflect bulk module conditions; localized microenvironments in crew sleeping quarters may exhibit micro-stratification.
attribution: NASA Ames Life Sciences Data Archive & OSDR (2024). Environmental Data App Telemetry Archive. NASA Ames Research Center.

sourceTitle: NASA Ongoing Exploration Medicine and Autonomous Health Research
researchSummary: Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC) research focuses on autonomous clinical decision support tools, offline medical registries, just-in-time clinical training, and physiological baseline monitoring for crewed Lunar Gateway and Mars transit missions where real-time Earth support is physically impossible.
limitations: Algorithms must maintain rigorous validation across multi-year uncrewed and crewed mission phases without continuous ground retraining.
attribution: NASA HRP Exploration Medical Capability Element (2024). Ongoing Research: Clinical Decision Support for Exploration Missions. NASA JSC.
